en: Cūḷaniddesa:
Exposition of the Pārāyaṇa Chapter;
Exposition of the Questions.
5. The Exposition of the Questions of the Young Brahmin Dhotaka "I ask you, Blessed One; please tell me this," [said the Venerable Dhotaka].
O Great Seer, I long for your voice;
having heard your sound,
I shall train myself for Nibbāna.
"I ask you, Blessed One, tell me.
"I ask" refers to three kinds of questions:
a question for the illumination of what has not been seen, a question for the confirmation of what has been seen, and a question for the cutting off of doubt... [and so forth].
These are the three questions...
[and so on] ...the question concerning Nibbāna. "I ask you" means: I ask you, I entreat you, I beseech you, I inspire confidence in you; "speak it to me."
"I ask you.
"Bhagavā" is a designation for reverence... [and so on] ...it is a designation based on realization, namely, "Bhagavā.
"Tell me": tell, declare, teach, describe, establish, reveal, analyze, make clear, and explain.
"I ask you, Blessed One, please tell me this.
Thus spoke the Venerable Dhotaka.
"Thus" (*iccā*) is a phonetic conjunction (*padasandhi*)... [etc.]
“Venerable” (*āyasmā*) is a term of endearment, a term of respect; it is a designation for one who possesses reverence and deference.

“Dhotaka” is the name, the designation, the appellation, the conventional usage, the name-giving, the naming, the title, the expression, the phrasing, and the utterance of that brahmin—thus he is called “the venerable Dhotaka.”

“I long for your word, O Great Seer”—I long for, yearn for, desire, accept, aspire to, cherish, and pray for your speech, your expression, your teaching, your instruction, and what has been instructed.
Why is the Blessed One called a “Great Seer” (*mahesi*)?
He is a Great Seer because he sought, searched for, and pursued the great aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*). … [and so on] …
“‘Where is the bull among men?’—O Great Seer, I long for your voice. Having heard your roar” means:

having heard your speech, your manner of expression, your teaching, your instruction, having heard what was instructed, having listened, having mastered it, having retained it, and having discerned it.
Having heard your cry,
"One should train for the sake of Nibbāna," as for "training":
there are three trainings.
The training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom …pe… this is the training in higher wisdom.
“Nibbāna for oneself” means for the extinguishing of one’s own lust.
for the extinguishing of hatred,
for the extinguishing of delusion,
for the extinguishing of anger.
For the extinguishing of resentment...

[and so on] ...for the equanimity, pacification, subsiding, extinguishing, relinquishment, and tranquilization of all unwholesome volitional formations, one should train in the higher virtue, one should train in the higher mind, and one should train in the higher wisdom.
One should train by being mindful of these three trainings.
One should train knowing,
one should train seeing,
one should train reflecting.
One should train by exerting the mind;
one should train by resolving with faith;
one should train by uplifting energy.
One should train in establishing mindfulness;
one should train in concentrating the mind;
one should train in understanding with wisdom.
One should train while directly knowing what is to be directly known;
one should train while fully understanding what is to be fully understood;
one should train while abandoning what is to be abandoned.
One should train by developing what is to be developed;
one should train by realizing what is to be realized;
one should practice, practice thoroughly, and conduct oneself having undertaken the training.
One should train for one’s own Nibbāna.
Therefore that brahmin said:
“I ask you, Blessed One, please tell me this:”
"Thus spoke the Venerable Dhotaka:
'O Great Seer, I long for your voice;
having heard your sound, [I am filled with joy].'"
“Train yourself for your own Nibbāna. Therefore,
O Dhota, exert yourself with diligence—
thus said the Blessed One.
Right here, being wise and mindful;
having heard this sound, one should train for one's own Nibbāna.
"Therefore, exert yourself" means: exert yourself; make an effort; make an endeavor; make strength;
make fortitude; make energy; generate desire, produce it, establish it, arouse it, bring it forth, and fully bring it forth.
"Therefore, exert yourself with diligence.
"Dhotaka," said the Blessed One, addressing that brahmin by name.
"Blessed" (*bhagavā*) is a term of reverence... [as above] ...it is a designation based on realization, namely, "the Blessed One."
"A cleanser," said the Blessed One.
"Right here, a wise person.
"Right here" means in this view, in this inclination, in this preference, in this adoption, and in this Dhamma.
In this discipline, in this Dhamma-discipline, in this teaching, in this holy life, in this instruction of the Teacher,
in this personal existence, in this human world.
"Nipaka" means one who is prudent, wise, possessed of wisdom, intelligent, knowledgeable, discerning, and sagacious.
"He is mindful" by way of four reasons:
one who develops the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the body as a body is mindful … [as before] … he is called "mindful."
"Right here, being wise and mindful.

Having heard from here the sound—that is, having heard my word, my manner of speech, my teaching, my instruction, and what was thus instructed; having heard it, learned it, retained it, reflected upon it, and discerned it—it is "having heard from here the sound."
"One should train for the sake of Nibbāna alone.
"Training" refers to the three trainings:
the training in higher virtue, the training in higher consciousness, and the training in higher wisdom... [and so forth].

This is the training in higher wisdom. One who considers only nibbāna as their goal should train in the higher virtue, the higher mind, and the higher wisdom for the extinguishing of their own lust, for the extinguishing of hatred, for the extinguishing of delusion, for the extinguishing of anger,

for the extinguishing of resentment— and so on— for the sake of the meeting, the pacifying, the calming, the extinguishing, the relinquishing, and the subsiding of all unwholesome volitional formations.
One should train by reflecting upon these three trainings; one should train knowing them...
[and so on] ...one should train realizing what is to be realized. One should practice them, practice them thoroughly, and conduct oneself having undertaken them—thus one trains for one’s own Nibbāna.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Therefore, exert yourself with ardor,
Dhota” (said the Blessed One).
Right here, being wise and mindful;
having heard this sound from here,
one should train for one's own Nibbāna.
In the world of gods and humans,
I see a brahmin wandering about, possessing nothing;
I pay homage to him, O All-Seeing One.
"O Sakka, release me from my doubts!
May I see the world of gods and humans. Regarding "gods," there are three kinds of gods: [the gods of the sense-sphere, the fine-material sphere, and the immaterial sphere].
There are conventional deities, deities by birth, and deities by purification.
Who are the conventional deities?
Conventional deities are said to be kings, princes, and queens.
These are called conventional deities (*sammutideva*).
Who are the deities by birth (*upapattideva*)?

The deities by birth are said to be the Cātumahārājika deities, the Tāvatiṃsa deities, the Yāma deities, the Tusita deities, the Nimmānarati deities, the Paranimmitavasavatti deities, the Brahmakāyika deities, and those deities who are even higher than these.
These are called the devas by rebirth.
Who are the devas of purification?
The devas of purification are said to be the Tathāgata’s disciples who are arahants with taints destroyed, as well as those who are paccekabuddhas.
These are called the devas of purification.

The Blessed One is the deva among the conventional devas, the devas by birth, and the devas of purification; he is the super-deva, the super-super-deva, the lion among lions, the elephant among elephants, the bull among bulls, the sage among sages, and the king among kings.

"I see a deva in the world of devas and humans"—in the human world, he sees a deva, he sees a super-deva, he sees a super-super-deva; he beholds him, looks upon him, contemplates him, and examines him.
"I see one who possesses nothing, a brahmin walking about in the world of gods and humans.

"Possessing nothing" means [free from] the possession of lust, the possession of hatred, the possession of delusion, the possession of conceit, the possession of views, and the possession of the defilements.

The "trifling things" of misconduct—the Blessed Buddha has abandoned these trifling things, cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, rendered them non-existent, so that they are subject to non-arising in the future; therefore, the Buddha is "possessing nothing.
The Blessed One is a "Brahmin" because he has banished seven qualities; thus he is a Brahmin.
The view of a personal body has been expelled; doubt has been expelled; clinging to rules and observances has been expelled;
lust has been expelled; hatred has been expelled; delusion has been expelled; conceit has been expelled.

Expelled from him are those evil, unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, and pertaining to future birth, aging, and death.
Having cast off all evils, Sabhiya—
so said the Blessed One—
you are stainless, well-composed, and firm in self.
"Having transcended *saṃsāra*, he is the absolute one;
unattached and such-like, he is called 'Brahmā'.
"Moving about" means walking, dwelling, moving, acting, maintaining, sustaining, or carrying on.
"I revere him, the one with all-seeing eyes, the Brahmin who possesses nothing as he goes along. Here,
"him" refers to the Blessed One.

"I pay homage" means: I pay homage with the body, or I pay homage with speech, or I pay homage with the mind, or I pay homage through practice in accordance with the goal, or I pay homage through practice in accordance with the Dhamma; I honor, revere, esteem, and worship.
"All-seeing eye" (samantacakkhu): "all-seeing eye" is a term for omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutañāṇa).
The Blessed One is endowed with, fully endowed with, has attained, fully attained, has reached, fully reached, is possessed of, and is fully possessed of omniscient knowledge.
“There is nothing here that he has not seen,
nor anything that is unknown or not to be known.”
The Tathāgata has directly known everything that is to be known;
by that he is the one with universal vision.
I pay homage to him, the one with universal vision.
"Release me from my doubts, O Sakka. Regarding "Sakka":
he is called Sakka because the Blessed One went forth from the Sakyan clan;
or alternatively, he is called Sakka because he is wealthy, possessing great riches and wealth.

These are his riches, namely: the riches of faith, the riches of virtue, the riches of moral shame, the riches of moral dread, the riches of learning, the riches of generosity, the riches of wisdom, the riches of the foundations of mindfulness,
the riches of the right efforts, the riches of the bases of psychic power, the riches of the faculties, the riches of the powers, and the riches of the factors of enlightenment.
The wealth of the path, the wealth of the fruit, and the wealth of Nibbāna.
Sakka is also called "the wealthy one" because he is rich, possessed of great riches, and endowed with these many kinds of treasures and jewels.

Alternatively, Sakka is so called because he is powerful, capable, self-sufficient, brave, heroic, valiant, fearless, undaunted, unafraid, not fleeing, having abandoned fear and terror, and being free from horripilation.
“Doubt” (kaṅkha) is said to be perplexity (vicikicchā).
It is doubt regarding suffering, doubt regarding the origin of suffering, doubt regarding the cessation of suffering, and doubt regarding the practice leading to the cessation of suffering;
it is doubt regarding the past, doubt regarding the future, doubt regarding both the past and the future, and doubt regarding phenomena that have arisen dependently through specific conditions.

Whatever such doubt, doubting, state of having doubted, perplexity, uncertainty, ambivalence, path of two ways, hesitation, grasping at various sides, shrinking back, shrinking forth, lack of penetration, trepidation of the mind, and mental distress—release me from these, Sakka!
"Release me from doubts": release me, set me free, liberate me, deliver me, uproot me, pull me out, raise me up from the thorn of doubt. Thus:
"Release me from doubts, Sakka!"
Therefore that brahmin said:
“I see in the world of gods and humans a brahmin wandering about, possessing nothing at all.”
"I pay homage to you, O All-Seeing One;
release me from my doubts, Sakka.
"I shall not be able to release you," he said.
O Dhota, having understood the supreme Dhamma, you have no more doubt regarding anything in the world;
thus you shall cross over this flood.
"I will not endure for the sake of release" means: "I am not able to release, set free, liberate, emancipate, extricate, fully extricate, raise up, or fully raise up [you] from the dart of doubt.
Thus, too, "I will not endure for the sake of release.
Or else, I do not strive, I do not exert myself, I do not persevere, I do not endeavor, I do not make an effort, I do not put forth energy.
"I shall not exert strength, I shall not exert fortitude, I shall not exert energy, I shall not generate desire, I shall not produce it, I shall not bring it forth,

I shall not fully bring it forth— toward those individuals who lack faith, who lack desire, who are indolent, deficient in energy, and who do not practice the teaching of the Dharma. Even in this way,
I will not be able to endure for the sake of their liberation.
Or rather, there is no one else at all who can release them.
Even if they were to release them by their own power, by their own strength, by their own energy,
by their own exertion, by their own human capacity, by their own human strength, by their own human energy, or by their own human exertion—
"May they, practicing themselves the right way, the conformable way, the unopposed way, the way that accords with the goal, the way that accords with the Dhamma,
be liberated. Even in this way, I would not be able to grant liberation.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Cunda, it is indeed impossible that one who is himself mired in the mire should lift up another who is mired in the mire.
Cunda, it is indeed impossible that one who is himself untamed, undisciplined, and not fully extinguished should tame another, discipline another, or lead another to full extinction.”
Even so, I shall not endure it for the sake of liberation.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
"The evil deed committed by oneself..."
By oneself one is defiled;
by oneself, through uncommitted evil,
one is purified.
"Purity and impurity are personal;
one cannot purify another.
Even thus, I will not grant you release.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
“In the same way, brahmin, Nibbāna stands, the path leading to Nibbāna stands, and I stand as one who encourages;
yet, even though my disciples are thus exhorted and thus instructed by me, some of them—”
“Some attain Nibbāna, the ultimate goal, while others do not.
“In this matter, what can I do, brahmin?
The Tathāgata, brahmin, is the proclaimer of the path.”
"The Buddha teaches the path so that those who practice it themselves may be liberated.
Even in this way, I would not be able to grant liberation.
Dhotaka, one who is wavering seeks out no one at all who is wavering—a person who is doubtful, hesitant, perplexed, and full of uncertainty.
"No one" means no one whatsoever: whether a khattiya, a brahmin, a vessa, a sudra; whether a householder or one gone forth; whether a deva or a human.
He seeks them in the world of the lower realms... [and so on] ...in the world of the sense bases.
"O Dhota, one who knows the supreme Dhamma has no more doubt regarding anything in the world.
Here, "the supreme Dhamma" refers to the deathless Nibbāna—
that which is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, and Nibbāna.
"Knowing, understanding, fully comprehending, and penetrating the Dhamma as supreme, foremost, best, preeminent, highest, and most excellent—
one who thus directly knows the supreme Dhamma:

'In this way you shall cross over this flood,' that is, you shall cross over, transcend, surmount, pass beyond, and go beyond the flood of sensual desire, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance."
In this way, you shall cross over this flood.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“I will not permit [your release] for the sake of liberation;”
“O Dhota, having abandoned all doubt in the world,
and having directly realized the supreme Dhamma,
may you thus cross over this flood.”
Instruct me, O Brahmā, out of compassion,
regarding the state of seclusion that I should understand,
so that I may remain untroubled like space.
"Right here, being peaceful, I would live unattached.
"Instruct me, O Brahmā; have compassion for me," means: instruct me, O Brahmā; favor me, O Brahmā; take pity on me, O Brahmā—thus, "instruct me, O Brahmā."
"Feeling compassion": feeling compassion, being sympathetic, protecting, favoring, and having pity.
"O Brahmā, teach with compassion":
that state of seclusion which I should understand is called the state of seclusion; it is the deathless Nibbāna.
"That which is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna—

that is what I would know, that I would come to know, that I would fully understand, that I would thoroughly understand, that I would penetrate, that I would attain, that I would touch, and that I would realize:
'I would know that state of seclusion.'"

"Just as I am unafflicted like space": just as space does not go forth, does not grasp, is not bound, and is not obstructed, so too, by not going forth, not grasping, not being bound, and not being obstructed—one is "unafflicted like space.
Just as space is not stained by lac, turmeric, indigo, or madder, so too, by not being stained, not being corrupted, not being deluded, and not being defiled—one is "unafflicted like space."
In this way too, space is non-afflictive.

Just as space does not become agitated, does not become afflicted, does not shrink back, and is not struck, so too, being unshakable, non-afflictive, not shrinking back, not being struck, and not being obstructed—
in this way too, space is non-afflictive.
"Let one live here itself, established and not dependent.
"Established here itself" means: being established right here, being seated right here, being seated on this very seat, being seated in this very assembly; thus it is "established here itself."
Or alternatively: "Being right here, serene, tranquil, extinguished, and calmed"—thus too it is "being right here.
"One who has eaten" refers to two supports:
The dependence on craving and the dependence on views... [as above] ...this is dependence on craving... [as above] ...this is dependence on views.

Having abandoned dependence on craving and relinquished dependence on views, one is not dependent on the eye, not dependent on the ear, not dependent on the nose, not dependent on the tongue, not dependent on the body, not dependent on the mind, [and not dependent on] forms...

In sounds … in odors … in tastes … in tangibles … in mental phenomena … in family … in group … in residence … in gain … in fame … in praise … in pleasure … in robes … in almsfood … in lodgings … in medicinal requisites for the sick … in the sense-sphere realm … in the fine-material realm … in the immaterial realm … in sensual existence … in fine-material existence … in immaterial existence …
He is not dependent on, not reliant on, not clinging to, not approaching, not attached to, not obsessed by,

and has emerged from and escaped from existence with perception … existence without perception … existence with neither-perception-nor-non-perception … one-constituent existence … four-constituent existence … five-constituent existence … the past … the future … the present;
he is not dependent on, not reliant on, not clinging to, not approaching, not attached to, not obsessed by, and has emerged from and escaped from phenomena that are seen, heard, sensed, and cognized.
"Completely free, detached, with a mind for which no boundaries exist"—
one should "wander" means one should move about, dwell, conduct oneself, behave, protect, maintain, sustain, and support [oneself]; that is, "right here,
being peaceful and independent, I shall wander."
Therefore that brahmin said:
“O Brahmā, out of compassion,
instruct me in the Dhamma of seclusion, which I may come to know.”
"Just as space is unafflicted, so may I,
being peaceful right here, wander without dependence.
I shall proclaim peace to you.
(“The Washerman,” said the Blessed One:
“That which is known in this very life, not based on tradition—
having understood this, one should live mindfully.”
Cross over the attachment to the world.
I shall describe to you peace: peace from lust, peace from hatred, peace from delusion, peace from anger, peace from resentment...
[and so on] ...peace from denigration, peace from spite, peace from envy, peace from stinginess, peace from deceit, peace from craftiness, peace from obstinacy.
… I shall praise, I shall extol, the peace, the pacification, the complete pacification, the extinction, and the subsiding of all agitation, of pride, of arrogance, of intoxication, of negligence,
of all defilements, of all misconduct, of all distress, of all fevers, of all torments, and of all unwholesome volitional formations.
"I shall declare it, I shall teach it, I shall describe it, I shall establish it, I shall reveal it, I shall analyze it, I shall make it plain, I shall illuminate it"—
thus I shall proclaim your peace,
O Dhotaka, said the Blessed One.
"Dhotaka," said the Blessed One, addressing that brahmin by name.
"Blessed One" (bhagavā) is a designation for reverence... [as before] ...it is a realization-designation (sacchikā paññatti), namely, "the Blessed One"—thus, "Dhotaka, Blessed One."
"Non-delusion regarding the seen phenomenon (*diṭṭhe dhamme anītihā*). "Regarding the seen phenomenon" means:
when the phenomenon is seen, known, weighed, scrutinized, fully understood, and manifested; [when one knows] that all conditioned things are impermanent...

[and so on] ...that whatever has the nature of arising, all that has the nature of cessation. Thus, it is "regarding the seen phenomenon," "known phenomenon," "weighed phenomenon," "scrutinized phenomenon," "fully understood phenomenon," and "manifested phenomenon. In this way also—

"In this very life... [as before]. Or alternatively: "When suffering is seen, I shall speak of suffering; when the origin is seen, I shall speak of the origin; when the path is seen, I shall speak of the path; when cessation is seen, I shall speak of cessation"—thus too, "in this very life... [as before].
Or alternatively: "It is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be realized by the wise each for themselves"—this too is "in this very life.
"Not based on hearsay" means not on the basis of "it is so," nor on tradition, nor on mere rumor, nor on the authority of scriptures, nor through ratiocination.
"I shall speak of that Dhamma which has been personally realized through direct higher knowledge by myself— not through logic,
nor through reasoning on the basis of forms, nor through acceptance of views after reflection—
but as something seen in this very life, not based on mere tradition."
Having understood that by which they live mindfully, having made it known, weighed it, scrutinized it, and fully clarified it;

having made it known, weighed it, scrutinized it, and fully clarified it that "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent"; [and] having made it known, weighed it, scrutinized it, and fully clarified it that "all conditioned phenomena are suffering"... [and so on].
“‘All phenomena are non-self’ …pe… ‘Whatever is subject to arising,
all that is subject to cessation’— having made this known, having weighed it, having scrutinized it, having analyzed it, and having made it manifest.
He is mindful by way of four reasons:”
Developing the foundation of mindfulness by contemplating the body as body, he is mindful...
[as before] ...he is called "mindful.
Walking, walking; dwelling, dwelling; acting, acting; performing, performing; protecting, protecting; maintaining, maintaining—he is thus called "mindful."
"Having understood this, one who dwells mindfully crosses over clinging in the world. Here, "clinging" (*visattikā*) is said to be craving (*taṇhā*).
It is lust, infatuation... [as before] ...covetousness, greed, the root of unwholesomeness.
"Entanglements": in what sense are they entanglements? ... [as above] ... they are spread out and extensive, thus they are "entanglements.
"In the world": in the world of the lower realms ... [as above] ... in the world of the sense bases.

"One should cross over the entanglements in the world": those entanglements are in the world; one should, being mindful, cross over, transcend, pass beyond, and surmount those entanglements in the world. Thus it is said.
Cross over attachment to the world.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“I shall describe peace to you.”
(The Blessed One said: "O Dhotaka,
that which is known in this very life, not based on tradition—
having understood this, one should live mindfully."
“Cross over the world’s attachment!”—
this supreme peace of the Great Seer, I too rejoice in.
Having understood that, practicing with mindfulness,
one may cross over attachment to the world;
that is what I rejoice in.

"I rejoice in, greatly delight in, am glad of, approve of, desire, accept, aspire to, long for, and yearn for those words of yours, your manner of speech, your teaching, and your instruction as it has been taught.
Thus, I rejoice in that.
"The supreme peace of the Great Seer."
Regarding "Mahesi": why is the Blessed One called Mahesi?
He is Mahesi because he sought, searched for, and pursued the great aggregate of virtue; [he is Mahesi] because he [sought] the great aggregate of concentration...
where is the Bull among Men? Thus he is Mahesi.
"Supreme peace": here "peace" (santi) refers to the deathless Nibbāna.
That which is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.
"Supreme" (uttama) means the foremost, the best, the most excellent, the preeminent, the highest, the most distinguished.
The Great Seer [attains] supreme peace.
Having understood this, they live mindfully; having made this known...
[as before] ...having made it known that "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent," having weighed it, scrutinized it, clarified it, and fully realized it;

“Having made known, weighed, scrutinized, clarified, and fully realized that ‘all conditioned phenomena are suffering,’ … ‘all phenomena are non-self,’ … and ‘whatever has the nature of arising, all that has the nature of cessation’;
he is mindful by way of four reasons.”
Developing the foundation of mindfulness by contemplating the body as a body, he is mindful...
[as before] ...he is called "mindful. While walking, he walks... [as before] ...he is called "mindful."
"Passing away"—
having understood this, one who dwells mindfully crosses over attachment to the world.
"Visattikā" (the clinging) is said to be craving.
It is that which is lust, infatuation, covetousness, greed, and the root of unwholesomeness.
In what sense is it called "visattikā"? ... It is called "visattikā" because it is spread out, extended, and diffused.
"In the world": in the world of the states of misery …pe… in the world of the sense bases.
"One should cross over attachment to the world" means: one should cross over, transcend, and pass beyond that attachment which is found in the world—that very attachment in the world;
mindful, one should cross over, transcend, and pass beyond it.
"Cross over attachment to the world.
Therefore that brahmin said:
"And that I do rejoice in."
The Great Seer has attained supreme peace;
having realized this, one who dwells mindful shall cross over attachment to the world.
"Whatever you perceive,
Dhota," said the Blessed One,
"above, below, across, and in between;"
Having understood this— that there is attachment in the world—
one should not form a craving for existence or non-existence.
"Whatever you are fully aware of" means whatever you are fully aware of, understand, comprehend, and penetrate.
"Whatever you perceive.
"Dhotaka," said the Blessed One.
"Dhotaka," the Blessed One addressed that brahmin by name.
"Bhagavā" is a designation for one who possesses reverence... [and so on] ...it is a realization-based designation, namely "Bhagavā"—thus the Blessed One is called "Dhotaka.
"Above, below, across, and in the middle."
He digs up the future;
he washes away the past;
and he levels the middle, which is the present.
Above is the world of the gods;
below is the world of the states of misery;
and across, in the middle, is the world of human beings.
Alternatively, "upward" refers to wholesome states (*kusalā dhammā*);
"downward" refers to unwholesome states (*akusalā dhammā*);
and "across and in the middle" refers to indeterminate states (*abyākatā dhammā*).
"Uddhaṃ" refers to the formless realm (arūpadhātu);
"adho" refers to the sense realm (kāmadhātu);
and "majjhe tiriyañca" refers to the form realm (rūpadhātu).
"Upward" refers to pleasant feeling;
"downward" refers to painful feeling;
and "across and in the middle" refers to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
"Uddhaṃ" means above the soles of the feet;
"adho" means below the tips of the hair;
and "tiriyam" as well as "majjhe" or "vemajjhe" means across the middle.
Above, below, across, and in the middle.

Having understood this as "attachment in the world"—knowing that this is attachment, that this is clinging, that this is a bond, that this is an impediment; having weighed it, known it, measured it, scrutinized it, and made it manifest—one understands:
"This is attachment in the world."
"Do not create craving for existence and non-existence.
"Craving" refers to craving for forms, craving for sounds, and so forth, up to craving for mental phenomena (*dhamma*).
"From existence to existence" means for the sake of becoming and non-becoming; for kamma-existence and renewed existence;
for sense-sphere existence, kamma-existence, renewed existence, and fine-material existence; for kamma-existence, fine-material existence, renewed existence, and immaterial existence;
for kamma-existence, immaterial existence, renewed existence, repeated existence, repeated destinies, and repeated rebirths.
"Do not create, do not generate, do not produce, do not bring about,
do not cause to arise craving for repeated rebirth and the repeated production of individual existence; abandon it, dispel it, bring it to an end, and lead it to non-existence"—
this is what is meant by "do not create craving for becoming after becoming."
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Whatever you perceive,
Dhota (said the Blessed One),"
Above, below, across, and in the middle—
having understood this world as a snare,
do not create craving for becoming and non-becoming.
With the conclusion of this verse... [as before] ...
"The Blessed One is my teacher, venerable sir; I am his disciple.
This is the fifth exposition: The Question of the Young Brahmin Dhotaka.
